newsitem.title: USA: U.S. concerned at Moscow action on Western drivers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. concerned at Moscow action on Western drivers.

text.p: U.S. embassy officials in Moscow have voiced concern to the Russian government over a recent spate of checks by traffic police on American and other Western drivers, the State Department said on Wednesday.
Spokesman Nicholas Burns said there were signs the Russian action was in retaliation for recently publicised problems faced by Russian diplomats driving in New York.

"Moscow traffic police have stopped American embassy employees, American diplomats, and a lot of...American journalists, Western journalists, with a very high degree of frequency over the last couple of days," Burns said.
"There have been lots of document checks and I even understand some policemen have made comments, 'Now you know how it feels to be a Russian living in New York'," he told a news briefing.
U.S. embassy officials had told Russian authorities of their concerns over the matter, Burns said.
"If there is an Operation Foreigner, we would respectfully hope that it would stop," he added.
The Russian and Belarus U.N. missions have been involved in a battle with New York city authorities over a fight on Dec. 29 between two of their diplomats and two policemen
The police said the diplomats attacked the officers after they were seen parked near a fire hydrant. The diplomats said they were attacked by the police.

New York mayor Rudolph Giuliani has also accused the two missions of failing to pay tens of thousands of dollars in parking fines. Russia's U.N. mission complained earlier this month that notes had been attached to many of its cars threatening to damage them over parking violations.
Burns said the State Department could assure Moscow that Russian diplomats were not being singled out on the streets of New York or Washington.
He said one thing Washington and Moscow did agree on was that diplomats abroad should obey that country's laws. "This can be resolved, I think, with a little goodwill on both sides," he added.
